claims: El Niño is characterized by the warming of ocean surface waters in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific.
El Niño typically occurs every 2 to 7 years.
El Niño causes intense rainfall in South America.
El Niño causes droughts in the West Pacific.
El Niño causes increased global temperatures.
El Niño is the warm phase of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) cycle.
El Niño occurs when trade winds weaken.
Trade winds weakening allows warm water to shift east towards South America.
The eastward shift of warm water towards South America prevents cold, nutrient-rich water from rising (upwelling).
La Niña is the opposite, colder phase of El Niño.
Scientists monitor the intensity of El Niño.
Very strong El Niño events are sometimes referred to as a "super El Niño".
A super El Niño can lead to record-breaking heat, such as in 2024.
El Niño can bring beneficial rain to the southern United States.
El Niño can bring beneficial rain to parts of Peru.
El Niño can reduce Atlantic hurricane activity.
El Niño is a natural phenomenon.
El Niño cannot be controlled.
NOAA monitors El Niño to forecast impacts on agriculture, fisheries, and infrastructure.
El Niño tends to increase global average temperatures.
El Niño leads to wetter conditions in the South of the United States.
El Niño leads to warmer/drier conditions in the North of the United States.
El Niño leads to heavy flooding in Peru/Ecuador.
El Niño leads to drought/wildfires in Australia
